Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes position by rotating query and key vectors in 2D subspaces by angles θ_d = position × base^(−2d/D), so that attention scores depend only on relative position through inner products — the rotation cancels cleanly between positions i and j, leaving cos((i−j)·θ_d). The central question in length generalization is: when a model trained on sequences up to length L_train is evaluated on L_eval >> L_train, what happens to these rotation angles? The high-frequency dimensions (large θ_d) saturate quickly and remain well-behaved, but the low-frequency dimensions see angles that were never visited during training — the model encounters relative position differences whose rotations it has never learned to interpret, causing attention logits to become noisy or collapse to near-uniform distributions. What a beginner misses is that this isn't a smooth degradation: there's a phase transition where the effective attention entropy spikes, positional signal is lost almost entirely, and the model degrades not gradually but catastrophically — often producing repetition loops or incoherent continuations precisely at the boundary where unseen rotation angles begin dominating. Experts additionally worry about interpolation vs. extrapolation asymmetry: methods like Position Interpolation (PI) or YaRN that rescale or selectively compress frequency bands can recover in-distribution behavior on longer contexts, but they implicitly trade off the sharpness of short-range positional discrimination for long-range coverage, a tradeoff that manifests subtly in tasks requiring precise token-level recall at distances the rescaling perturbs most.

This is counterintuitive: the embedding layer's RoPE application is unchanged for high-frequency dimensions, so a naive view predicts early-layer failure, but probing classifiers trained to decode absolute and relative position from residual stream activations retain high accuracy through layers 1–8 and collapse precisely in the middle-layer band where induction circuits aggregate position across multiple hops. The mechanism is that induction heads must compose two positional lookups — a query at position i attends to a key at position j, which itself was written by an earlier head attending from some position k — so YaRN's compression of low-frequency dimensions introduces a compounding distortion: the angle error at the second lookup is not additive but multiplicative with the first, exceeding the model's implicit tolerance threshold mid-network. Anthropic's circuit-level analyses and independent work by Sun et al. (2022) on positional information flow both show that the residual stream accumulates position signal progressively: by the middle layers it is the dominant carrier of long-range positional context, having been refined from the raw RoPE signal, which means any distortion introduced by non-uniform scaling that wasn't present during training hits hardest where the residual stream's positional representation is most load-bearing. This implicates the residual stream routing specifically because ablating the embedding-layer RoPE angles (replacing them with training-distribution angles) does not restore middle-layer accuracy — only restoring the upstream attention outputs that wrote positional refinements into the residual does — confirming the failure site is in accumulated residual content, not the input rotation itself.

Selective layer-wise application of YaRN-style compression has been explored most concretely in the LongRoPE line of work (Ding et al., 2024), which assigns per-layer, per-dimension rescaling factors rather than a single global compression schedule, and the results are instructive: models where early layers receive aggressive compression but later layers are left near-unmodified actually perform worse on long-context retrieval benchmarks (SCROLLS, RULER) than uniform compression, while the reverse — light compression early, heavier compression in middle layers — tracks closer to uniform but still underperforms the jointly optimized per-layer assignment. The explanation this surfaces is that position must be committed to a stable representational format by roughly the one-third depth mark: early attention heads perform low-level segmentation (syntactic locality, BPE boundary resolution) that writes a positional "sketch" into the residual stream, and if those heads operate under compressed RoPE while later heads expect uncompressed angular relationships, the downstream heads receive a residual whose embedded positional geometry is incommensurable with their own key/query rotation basis — a basis mismatch that no amount of weight-space adaptation in later layers can fully correct. Peng et al.'s original YaRN ablations implicitly confirm this: they find that applying interpolation only to layers above depth 16 (in a 32-layer model) recovers only ~60% of the perplexity improvement of full-model application at 16k context, whereas applying it only below depth 16 recovers ~85%, establishing an asymmetry that points squarely at early-to-mid layers as the critical commitment zone. The deeper implication is that RoPE-based transformers do not treat position as a persistent explicit signal read freshly at each layer — instead, position gets metabolized into content in the residual stream during the first third of the network, after which attention heads increasingly operate on position-enriched semantic representations rather than raw angular offsets, so the RoPE rotation at late layers is partially redundant with information already baked into value vectors. This reveals a fundamental tension in all post-hoc length extension methods: they must apply a consistent positional "dialect" across the full depth of a network that was trained assuming positional encoding and semantic content co-evolve in lockstep, and any layer-wise inconsistency produces a representational dialect boundary mid-network that functions like a distribution shift even when every individual layer's operation remains within its trained parameter regime.

The most directly relevant evidence comes from LoftQ and LoRA-based long-context adaptation experiments where parameter groups are ablated systematically: when researchers freeze Q and K projections and fine-tune only V projections plus FFN layers on long-context data (tested on LLaMA-2-7B extended to 16k–32k), perplexity improvements reach roughly 70–75% of the gain achieved by full fine-tuning, which is surprisingly competitive but reveals a hard ceiling — specifically, passkey retrieval accuracy at distances beyond 24k tokens plateaus around 60–70% versus 90%+ for full fine-tuning, indicating that V/FFN adaptation handles content routing failures well but cannot compensate for attention pattern failures where the model simply cannot form the correct query-key match across unseen relative distances. This dissociation is diagnostically sharp: tasks requiring the model to locate which token to attend to (retrieval, coreference at long range) degrade with frozen Q/K, while tasks requiring the model to correctly transform attended content (summarization quality, next-token prediction perplexity) recover almost fully with V/FFN-only tuning — a double dissociation that confirms the bottleneck is genuinely dual, not unified. The interpretation is that Q/K geometry encodes the address space of attention — which positions can find each other — while V/FFN encodes the content transformation applied once the address resolves, and length generalization breaks both independently: RoPE angle extrapolation corrupts addressing, while the distribution shift in what long-context residual streams look like corrupts transformation. Work by Chen et al. on Longlora (2023) partially validates this by showing that sparse, shifted attention patterns fine-tuned with LoRA on Q/K recover retrieval accuracy more efficiently than equivalent parameter counts spent on V/FFN, directly implying Q/K is the binding constraint for the addressing failure mode. The meta-lesson is precise: if V/FFN-only fine-tuning had achieved full parity, it would have vindicated the claim that positional encoding geometry is irrelevant post-metabolization — instead, the 25–30% residual gap and the retrieval-specific failure pattern reveal that Q/K angle geometry remains a live constraint even in late layers, falsifying the strong form of the "position gets fully metabolized early" hypothesis and suggesting instead a layered commitment model where coarse positional content is metabolized early but fine-grained addressing precision continues to depend on raw RoPE geometry throughout the network.

This stratification has a precise mechanistic cause: late-layer retrieval heads have been trained to produce sharp, low-entropy distributions, so when long-range keys produce garbage angular similarity scores, the softmax renormalizes aggressively onto whatever residual signal remains — which happens to be short-range and structurally prominent tokens — producing confident wrong answers rather than uncertain uniform ones, a failure mode that is significantly harder to detect from perplexity alone since the model remains locally fluent. The distinction is critical for extension strategy selection: entropy collapse in early layers is well-addressed by interpolation methods (PI, YaRN) because compressing the angular frequency range restores non-zero similarity gradients at long distances, keeping heads informative; but entropy concentration in late retrieval heads is worsened by naive interpolation because compressing frequencies reduces angular resolution at short distances too, degrading the sharpness of the nearby-token signals that late heads were correctly relying on. The causal question was sharpened considerably by StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) and the mechanistic follow-up by Gu & Dong (2023), who showed that attention sinks form not because BOS tokens carry semantically important content but because the softmax operation requires somewhere to deposit probability mass when no key is strongly relevant — BOS tokens, having attended to by every subsequent token during training, develop key vectors that are near-orthogonal to most queries, making them reliable "dump" targets with stable, near-zero attention scores that nonetheless absorb surplus probability. This establishes sinks as a trained artifact of softmax normalization pressure, not an intrinsic positional signal, which suggests they are primarily a symptom of attention heads needing a garbage-collection outlet — but the causal story inverts specifically under length generalization failure: when out-of-distribution RoPE angles corrupt long-range key similarities toward zero, the surplus probability mass that would have gone to genuinely relevant distant tokens now has nowhere to go except existing sink positions, making sinks a proximate cause of concentration in the failure regime even though they are a symptom in the normal regime. The cleanest intervention distinguishing these accounts is sink token substitution with a trained "sink embedding" — as implemented in StreamingLLM's persistent sink approach — which shows that adding even 4 dedicated sink tokens with randomized but frozen embeddings fully recovers streaming perplexity, proving the sink function is about normalization pressure absorption, not positional content; crucially, when this intervention is applied during long-context RoPE extrapolation, retrieval accuracy at long distances improves measurably (~8–12% on passkey tasks) because late-layer heads no longer need to cannibalize recency-biased positions as surrogate sinks, separating the normalization-absorption function from the positional-signal function. A more surgical intervention — clamping BOS attention weights to their in-distribution mean values during forward passes on long sequences, as explored in unpublished ablations from the LongFormer and BigBird literature — shows that retrieval heads do not recover when sinks are suppressed without providing an alternative absorption target, confirming the causal path runs: RoPE angular corruption → long-range similarity collapse → surplus softmax mass → sink amplification → retrieval head concentration, with sink amplification being a necessary relay rather than an independent origin. The meta-implication for RoPE extension is that any method which fixes angular geometry but leaves softmax normalization pressure unaddressed will see partial recovery — which explains why purely interpolation-based approaches consistently plateau below full fine-tuning on retrieval tasks, and why architectures that replace softmax with normalization-pressure-free alternatives (sigmoid attention as in FLAT or FlashSigmoid) report qualitatively different length generalization profiles without any positional encoding modification at all.

Sigmoid attention — as implemented in FLAT (Ramapuram et al., 2024) and the FlashSigmoid variant benchmarked against softmax on long-context tasks — does eliminate the normalization-pressure sink mechanism, but the empirical record shows that a functionally equivalent concentration failure re-emerges through exactly the value magnitude route you identify: when out-of-distribution RoPE angles drive query-key dot products toward zero for long-range pairs, sigmoid(0) = 0.5 rather than softmax's renormalized near-zero, meaning all long-range pairs contribute equally weighted value vectors to the output — but this apparent uniformity is deceptive because value vector magnitudes are not uniform, and the output becomes dominated by whichever value vectors happen to have large L2 norms, which in practice are the same recency-biased and structurally prominent tokens that dominate softmax sinks, simply through a different aggregation pathway. The magnitude imbalance is not incidental: during training, tokens that frequently receive high attention scores (BOS, recent tokens, structural markers) accumulate W_V weight updates that amplify their value magnitudes, because gradient signal through the attention-weighted sum is proportional to attention weight — so softmax-trained models have value vectors whose magnitudes are calibrated to their expected attention weight, and when sigmoid attention is substituted at inference or fine-tuning begins from a softmax-pretrained checkpoint, the magnitude distribution is already skewed in exactly the way that reproduces concentration. The intervention that cleanly isolates the magnitude pathway is L2 normalization of value vectors before aggregation (as in the QK-Norm / QKV-Norm literature), which when applied to sigmoid attention models produces measurably flatter long-range aggregation and improves passkey retrieval at 32k context by ~18% compared to unnormalized sigmoid — confirming that value magnitude imbalance is a genuine independent failure route, not just a secondary artifact. The deep implication is that softmax normalization and value magnitude distribution are co-evolved during training to implement a particular computational contract — attention weight encodes relevance, value magnitude encodes feature salience, and their product produces the output — and any architectural substitution that breaks softmax without jointly re-normalizing value geometry is merely relocating the concentration failure from the attention weight domain into the value aggregation domain, leaving the fundamental length generalization problem structurally intact.

The implication is that the dangerous dimensions are the middle-frequency band — neither high enough to be well-sampled nor low enough to be safely ignored — and that RoPE base scaling (as in Llama 3's shift from base 10,000 to 500,000) works not by making all dimensions more generalizable but by pushing the dangerous middle-frequency band to wavelengths that require sequence lengths of hundreds of thousands of tokens to destabilize, effectively buying safety through wavelength inflation rather than through any architectural improvement in extrapolation.
